ANSWER: a

The best read is that his B is fully committed and predictable early: by the time a late B execute comes, he has already used his smoke, molotov and HE, so B is much easier to take. The other options are weaker because “contacting him early” does not reliably beat a player who is safe and using utility to block angles, going short alone does not exploit his spent utility and can be a bad 1v1, and “smoke the molotov and pop out” is not a clean or reliable play against early B control.

ANSWER: b

**Why b is best:** It nails both halves. The micro matches the described play exactly — jiggling A main is spotting the angle early, and "instantly blocks on contact" is throwing the pre-dropped smoke the moment he confirms a T is entering, i.e. block utility used on confirmation, not a static hold. The macro then explains the *why*: the 4-man B stack, the two smokes existing as block utility for the solo A, the expected payoff (2–3 kills if FaZe push through the smoke while bunched), and the fallback (buys rotation time to take the rest of the map on an execute). That is a complete micro + macro read.

**Why the others are worse:**
- **d** has the correct micro but its macro is just a bare restatement of a fact from the prompt ("stack B with 4 players"). It gives no reasoning for the smokes or the expected outcome, so it is an observation, not an analysis — incomplete for what the question asks.
- **a** has the wrong micro (says Krimz "stands close A main ready to take on any defenders," which contradicts the block-on-contact play) and a vague macro that never explains the B stack or what the two smokes are actually for.
- **c** points the micro at the B players instead of Krimz (off-topic for the described micro), and its macro cites a fabricated stat ("FaZe went B in 9 out of 10 antiecos") that is not in the scenario and doesn't fit the situation.

ANSWER: c

This fits best because the FNATIC eco setup is unbalanced: four on B and only KRIMZ on A. As FaZe, the cleanest way to win is to start with a split default to confirm where the stack is, then hit the undermanned side. In this case, seeing the B stack means going A, where the single defender can be overwhelmed with numbers and utility.

a is worse because a fake execute can waste time and utility; the main goal is to confirm the imbalance and attack the lesser response. b is too passive for an anti-eco round, letting the eco CT hold angles and force mistakes. d is too generic and does not address the specific stacked eco setup.

ANSWER: d

Option d is the best antistrat set because it converts the observed Spirit patterns into concrete, actionable counters: a Heaven fight tells you they likely started 3 mid, so you need to execute or react quickly before they can re-position; their single flash with no follow-up gives you a clear moment to pop mid; and a 4A/1B or 4B/1Mid default lets you keep a strong stack while one player takes early information.

Option a is worse because it overstates the value of an instant B contact and ignores that one of the rounds had a 1-mid/4-B start, so “never 4B” is not supported. Option b is too passive and not well backed by only five early rounds; “never push elbow” and “laterounds are extremely advantageous” are thin conclusions. Option c is reasonable in spirit but too generic and less precise: nading mid and giving up mid fights is a safe default, but it misses the clearer reads in d about Heaven pressure, the single flash, and how to structure the default.

ANSWER: b

Option b directly fixes each of the three defects you found: missing round IDs get traceable evidence, "always" claims get softened to match the actual exception rate, and CT/T-mixed behaviors get split into side-specific entries. The final re-check against source rounds closes the loop so the corrections are verified, not just asserted.

- **a** is the "themes are probably right" trap. 8 of 20 claims (40%) have no evidence, 2 overstate, and 3 conflate the two most fundamental axes of CS2 behavior. A user acting on mixed-side or unsupported claims will prepare the wrong anti-strat.
- **c** removes the only thing that makes a claim checkable. The problem is missing IDs, not too many; stripping the rest makes the report unverifiable and doesn't touch the "always" or side-mixing issues.
- **d** increases confidence on top of missing or wrong evidence, which is the worst combination: the reader trusts the claim more precisely because it sounds certain, while the underlying data is absent or incorrect.

ANSWER: a

The best correction is to reclassify it as B presence/default transitioning to A, because the video shows a split setup rather than a committed B execute: only two players are actually holding B main, one watches mid, one lurks connector, and the bomb carrier rotates A after CT utility. A genuine B execute normally requires clear commitment to take B, such as utility into B, coordinated entry, or a forced A/B split that is still aimed at B.

Option b is worse because calling it a “failed B execute” assumes the team intended to execute B, which the video does not support. Option c is worse because the round is still useful tactical data; it just needs the correct label. Option d is worse because player count near B at one moment is not enough to prove a B execute; position alone can describe presence, not intent.

The practical counter is also right: pressure him with coordinated support rather than isolated dry peeks.

Option b is wrong because it says he never takes opening duels, which contradicts the 70% figure. Option c is wrong because it repeats the unsupported “aggressive” label and suggests challenging him early in a way the demo behavior does not justify. Option d is wrong because “always saves his AWP” contradicts the fact that he is using it in most opening duels.

ANSWER: a

b is wrong because simply staying mid does not make a round a split. c is wrong because there is no A execute or fake A described. d is wrong because any lurker does not automatically create a split; the attacking lanes and coordinated entry matter.

ANSWER: c

This is the correct treatment because the reported trigger is “rotate to A after B utility,” so only rounds where B utility could plausibly cause the rotation should be included in that specific trigger metric. Rounds where A was already planted before the player moved are not rotations caused by B utility; they are post-plant retake or repositioning movements and should be analysed separately.

Option a is wrong because keeping 9/12 mixes two different causal situations and overstates the trigger rate. Option b is worse because it ignores timing and context entirely, turning a trigger metric into a generic “moved to A” count. Option d is wrong because deleting valid rounds destroys data; those rounds are still useful, just not for measuring the B-utility rotation trigger.

ANSWER: c

The best read is that his B utility is fully spent before 1:35, so if you delay your B execute he has no smoke, molotov, or HE left to contest the push. That makes late B the most reliable exploit.

a) is worse because contacting B early puts you into the window where he is using that utility, so he likely has the advantage early, not a free kill.

b) is worse because going short alone is risky and does not exploit the main tell; his short player being far away is secondary to the fact that the anchor will be utilityless later.

d) is worse because it focuses on early B control, but the clear pattern is that his utility is gone by lateround, so playing late is the stronger and safer counter.

ANSWER: b

**Why b is best:**
The micro nails the specific behavior described — KRIMZ spots A main early using his block utility (the 2 dropped smokes) and throws one the instant he gets confirmation Ts are entering, which is exactly what "jiggling A main and instantly blocks on contact" means. The macro then explains the full logic: FNATIC stack B with 4 and hand the solo A player 2 smokes to block with. On an eco, the smoke-limited fight levels the gun gap, so KRIMZ is good for 2–3 kills if FaZe push through; if the block fails, it buys time for the B stack to rotate and take the rest of the map. That is a complete, coherent micro + macro read.

**Why the others are worse:**
- **a)** The micro describes the *B players'* positioning (staying close to maximize weak-gun advantage in crossfires), not KRIMZ's action, which is the focus of the question. The macro leans on an unverifiable stat ("9 out of 10 of the last antiecos") and never explains what the 2 smokes are actually for.
- **c)** The micro is vague ("stands close A main ready to take on any defenders") and misses the jiggling/block-on-confirmation behavior entirely. The macro is weak — "have the enemy fear going into the bombsite" is not a real tactical rationale and ignores the rotation/buy-time logic.
- **d)** The micro is correct (identical to b), but the macro is a bare fact — "FNATIC stack B with 4 players" — with no explanation of why they stack or what the smokes accomplish. It stops at observation and never reaches analysis, so it is incomplete compared to b.

ANSWER: d

In an anti-eco, the T side has the utility and economy advantage, so the best approach is to force a response with a fake, take information on the other side, and then execute where the CT response is weaker. In the example, that means faking the B stack and then hitting A, where only KRIMZ is holding with smokes. Option a is too passive and gives the eco time to set up. Option b is too vague: quality matters, but “any strategy” is not a reliable doctrine. Option c is reasonable, but it is more passive and binary; a fake makes the execute safer by forcing the CT to commit or reveal their response before you go where they are weakest.

ANSWER: d

**Why d is best:** All three notes are specific, actionable, and directly tied to the dominant patterns in the five rounds. Note 1 links the heaven push to the 3-mid start (seen in rounds 1, 2, 3, and 5) and gives a concrete 10-second window to react on sites before they rotate. Note 2 identifies that Spirit throws exactly one flash on mid in four of the five rounds and never a follow-up, so popping out after that single flash is a clean, repeatable counter. Note 3 gives a clear default structure (4A 1B or 4B 1Mid) that lets the lone mid player read the heaven push and trigger an instant site reaction. Together they tell a T-side player exactly what to look for, when to act, and how to set up.

**Why the others are worse:**

- **a** – "Playing slow and calming down" in a heaven fight is vague and doesn't give a clear action. The nade-stack heaven tip is reasonable but only applies to the first round, not the pattern. "Giving up mid fights" contradicts what the rounds show: Spirit actively clears mid with utility in 4 of 5 rounds, so the threat is the mid/heaven push, not a passive mid hold.
- **b** – The one-flash observation is valid, and the B-rush point is true (no round starts 4B), but "going out mid is necessary" is less precise than d's timed reaction guidance. The B-rush note is a secondary exploit; the primary threat in 4 of 5 rounds is the mid-to-heaven push, which b doesn't address with a concrete counter.
- **c** – "Not an option" and "never push down elbow" are too absolute and not clearly supported by the five rounds (round 3 does smoke elbow and check early). "Playing the laterounds is extremely advantageous" is vague and not tied to any specific observed pattern, making it a weak antistrat line.

ANSWER: a

The issues are traceability, overconfidence, and side contamination, so the fix is to make each claim evidence-backed, appropriately qualified, and side-specific before delivery.

b is worse because removing round IDs destroys the audit trail and makes the tendencies harder to trust.  
c is worse because delivering known unsupported, overstated, or mixed-side claims risks misleading the coach and players.  
d is worse because more confident prose would make the same errors sound stronger, not fix them.

ANSWER: d

The video shows a B presence or default setup, not a committed B execute: only two players are actually holding B main, one is watching mid, one is lurking connector, and the bomb carrier later rotates A after CT utility. A B execute should show a clear pre-rotation commitment to B, such as coordinated utility, entry timing, and a plan to take B before rotating.

- a is worse because player count near B is not enough; “near B” can include loose positioning, lurks, or presence without a real execute.
- b is worse because it was not a failed B execute; the round does not show a genuine B execute that was denied.
- c is worse because the round is still useful tactical data; it should be corrected, not deleted.

ANSWER: c

Option c is best because it keeps the measurable fact — M often starts duels with an AWP — while correcting the misleading “aggressive” label with the observed behavior: safe angles, little re-peeking, and backing off without support. It also gives a useful counter-strategy: apply coordinated pressure instead of isolated dry peeks.

Option a is wrong because “always saves his AWP” contradicts the 70% opening-duel stat and is too absolute. Option b is wrong because “never takes opening duels” is false; he takes many of them. Option d is the weakest because it repeats the tool’s inaccurate summary and recommends a response that ignores the demo evidence.

ANSWER: c

It is best because a true “B split” requires coordinated entry into B from more than one route, such as B main plus water/connector or another second lane. Here the only B entry comes from B main, while the two mid players are controlling rotations or lurking, so the round is a B main execute with mid rotation-control/lurk roles.

a is wrong because a lurker does not automatically make a split; the definition depends on the target-site entry routes, not merely having players off the main push.

b is wrong because staying mid is not the same as splitting B; those players are not entering B from a second coordinated route.

d is wrong because there is no described A entry, A utility, or A-side action that would support calling it a fake A execute.

ANSWER: a

The reported trigger is "B utility causes the rotation to A," so the metric is only valid in rounds where B utility could actually be the cause. In the four rounds where A was already planted before the player moved, the plant — not B utility — is what drives his movement to A, so those are retake responses, not trigger rotations. The correct treatment is to split pre-execute rotations from post-plant retakes and recompute the trigger rate on the subset where the trigger is still possible; the four rounds stay in the data, they just don't count toward this one metric (they're valid evidence for a retake metric instead).

- b) Keeping 9/12 is wrong because it lumps two different causes into one number, inflating and distorting the trigger rate with rounds where the trigger couldn't have fired.
- c) Deleting the four rounds from the database is wrong — you never destroy raw data; you exclude rounds from a specific calculation. Those rounds are still legitimate for other metrics.
- d) Counting every movement to A regardless of timing is the worst option: it doesn't even separate the trigger from the retake, so the number stops measuring the claimed behaviour at all.
